screens.title: Why Redis needs persistence
screens.narratorSegment: Redis stores data in memory for speed, but R A M is volatile. If the server crashes or is shut down improperly, data in memory will be lost unless Redis writes state to non-volatile storage. Persistence bridges this gap by ensuring written state survives process restarts and machine failures. There are two primary mechanisms in Redis: RDB snapshots and the Append-Only File. Each takes a different approach. RDB captures a compact point-in-time image of the entire dataset. The result is a single binary snapshot that is fast to load and efficient for backups. AOF, by contrast, records every write command received by the server and replays those commands on restart so the dataset is reconstructed exactly as operations were applied. A common misconception is that enabling any persistence removes all recovery risk; in reality each method offers different guarantees and costs. For example, RDB can lose changes made after the last snapshot, while AOF can be tuned to reduce that window down to zero with higher input and output cost. Understanding this trade-off is the first practical step toward selecting the right configuration for your application.

content.html:
Core Concept › Why Redis needs persistence

Persistence: definition and role

Persistence ensures that data held in RAM is written to a non-volatile medium so it can survive restarts and crashes. Redis provides RDB and AOF for this purpose.

RDB (snapshot)
Compact binary snapshot of the full dataset at a point in time.
AOF (append-only)
Text log of every write command; replayed to rebuild dataset.
Key Takeaway

No single persistence mode fits all needs. Choose based on acceptable data-loss window and performance trade-offs.

Concrete example

A chat application can tolerate short data loss for ephemeral messages and might use RDB. A banking ledger cannot — AOF or AOF with always fsync is more appropriate.

Common misconception

Turning on AOF automatically makes performance identical to no persistence. In fact, fsync policy affects throughput and latency; choose deliberately.

Why this matters

Understanding persistence prevents accidental data loss, informs hardware choices, and sets expectations for restart and recovery times during incidents.

screens.title: How RDB snapshots work
screens.narratorSegment: RDB persists data by creating point-in-time snapshots using a forked child process. When a snapshot is triggered — by a save directive or BGSAVE — the main Redis process forks. The child process serializes the in-memory dataset and writes it to a temporary RDB file on disk. Because of copy-on-write semantics, the parent can continue serving requests while the child performs disk input and output. After the child finishes writing, Redis atomically replaces the old RDB file with the new one. This makes RDB snapshots C P U- and IO-efficient for periodic backups and fast restarts. A key advantage is that the resulting file is compact and quick to load at startup. A key limitation is the data-loss window: any writes after the last snapshot and before a crash are not persisted. Also, frequent snapshots increase disk input and output and the number of forks, which increases C P U usage. For testing you can use save directives like save 900 1 and run BGSAVE manually. Remember a blocking SAVE call will stop the server, so BGSAVE is preferred in production. This explanation clarifies why RDB is ideal for periodic backups, not continuous durability.

keyIdea.title: RDB snapshot flow
keyIdea.text: Trigger → fork child → child writes temp RDB → replace old file. Parent continues serving; snapshots are compact but can lose recent writes.

content.html:
Process Flow › How RDB snapshots work

Snapshot lifecycle

  1. Trigger by save rules or BGSAVE command.
  2. The server calls fork() to create a child process.
  3. The child serializes memory and writes a temporary RDB file.
  4. On completion the temporary file replaces the prior dump.rdb atomically.
  5. Parent process continues serving clients while child writes.
Concrete example
Run BGSAVE; check that a child process performs the write and dump.rdb timestamp updates afterwards.
Warning
Frequent snapshots increase fork activity and disk I/O; tune save directives for your workload.
Visualized sequence
Trigger → fork → child writes temp file → rename to dump.rdb
Example command
BGSAVE
Use BGSAVE in production to avoid blocking.
Key Takeaway

RDB is efficient for backups and fast restarts, but snapshots create a data-loss window between saves.

screens.title: Configuring RDB with save directives
screens.narratorSegment: RDB is configured with save directives inside redis. conf. Each directive expresses a rule: save. For example, save 900 1 means if at least one key changed within 900 seconds, take a snapshot. You can include multiple save lines to cover different workloads, for instance save 300 10 to capture more frequent changes when many keys update. When designing save rules, balance frequency and overhead: more frequent snapshots reduce your data-loss window but increase disk input and output and C P U work from forking. For testing, set very short rules such as save 5 1 so snapshots occur quickly. Never use the SAVE command in production, because it blocks the server; use BGSAVE instead. When editing redis. conf, also set dbfilename and dir so you know where dump. rdb will land. A common error is editing the wrong config file or forgetting to restart Redis with the modified file. Always verify dump. rdb timestamps after triggering BGSAVE to confirm the snapshot occurred. Configuring RDB with save directives means use save <seconds> <changes> rules in redis.conf and prefer bgsave for background snapshots; balance frequency against resource use.. In practical terms, how to write rules that trigger snapshots. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Configuring RDB

Save directive pattern

Each save line uses two numbers: seconds and number of changes that trigger a snapshot.

# Example RDB configuration in redis.conf save 900 1 # Save if 1 key changed in 15 minutes save 300 10 # Save if 10 keys changed in 5 minutes save 60 10000 # Save if 10000 keys changed in 1 minute # Manual BGSAVE command in redis-cli BGSAVE
Tips
  • Use BGSAVE to avoid blocking clients.
  • Short intervals for tests; longer for production workloads.
  • Confirm dump.rdb timestamp after saves.
Example scenario

For a low-traffic cache you might accept save 900 1. For an admin dashboard with bursts, add a medium-frequency rule to capture changes faster.

Common mistake

Editing redis.conf but not starting Redis with that file or forgetting file paths so you cannot find dump.rdb.

Why it matters

Save rules determine how much recent data you risk losing. Tune rules to match acceptable risk and resource limits.

screens.title: SAVE vs BGSAVE
screens.narratorSegment: Redis supports two snapshot commands with very different operational effects. SAVE writes a snapshot synchronously: the server stops serving clients while it writes dump. rdb. Because of that blocking behavior, SAVE is not recommended in production unless you can tolerate pauses. BGSAVE forks a child process and saves the snapshot in the background, allowing the parent to continue handling requests. The child performs the heavy disk input and output while copy-on-write preserves consistency. A misconception is that both are equivalent except for speed; in reality SAVE can disrupt latency-sensitive services and should be reserved for controlled maintenance windows. BGSAVE has its own costs: each fork increases memory pressure because of copy-on-write, and if the server is already near memory limits, a fork can fail. Use BGSAVE for routine snapshots and plan snapshot frequency to avoid overloading the system. When you need an immediate snapshot for debugging, ensure you understand the production impact before using SAVE. SAVE vs BGSAVE means save blocks the server until completion. bgsave forks a child and runs in the background; prefer bgsave in production unless you accept blocking.. In practical terms, blocking vs background snapshot commands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › SAVE vs BGSAVE

Blocking versus background

SAVE
  • Synchronous snapshot that blocks clients.
  • Useful for controlled maintenance or debugging.
  • Not recommended for latency-sensitive production use.
BGSAVE
  • Forks child process to save snapshot in background.
  • Parent continues serving requests during write.
  • Consumes extra memory due to copy-on-write semantics.
Concrete example

In a production API with tight latency SLOs, run BGSAVE during low-traffic windows and avoid SAVE to prevent service interruptions.

Common mistake

Running SAVE without planning causes unexpected downtime and client errors.

Check your environment

Ensure adequate free memory before frequent forks and watch fork failures as a signal to adjust snapshot frequency.

screens.title: RDB advantages and disadvantages
screens.narratorSegment: RDB snapshots are compact, fast to load, and excellent for backups and disaster recovery. Because they store a binary representation of the whole dataset, loading dump. rdb at startup reconstructs data quickly from a single file. This makes RDB a great choice when you need periodic backups, want a compact file to transfer between systems, or need fast restart times. The main disadvantage is durability: any writes made after the last snapshot and before a crash will be lost. You can reduce that window by taking snapshots more often, but that increases C P U and disk activity. Another risk is that frequent forks increase memory pressure due to copy-on-write and can create performance spikes. Common use cases for RDB include scheduled backups, exporting datasets, and environments where occasional small data loss is acceptable, such as caches or analytics that can be recomputed. A misconception is treating RDB as sufficient for all production durability needs — for strong durability guarantees, combine RDB with AOF or tune AOF for your workload. RDB advantages and disadvantages means choose rdb for compact backups and fast restarts if occasional data loss is acceptable; avoid relying on snapshots alone for strict durability.. In practical terms, when to use snapshots and what to watch for. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › RDB pros & cons

Advantages

  • Compact binary files ideal for backups and transfers.
  • Fast restart because dataset loads from a single optimized file.
  • Lower runtime overhead when snapshots are infrequent.

Disadvantages

  • Data-loss window between snapshots.
  • Frequent snapshots increase CPU and disk I/O from forks.
  • Not designed for continuous durability guarantees.
Example use cases

Backups, disaster recovery, migrations, and caches where occasional loss is acceptable.

Pro tip

Store dump.rdb on reliable, fast storage and monitor timestamps to confirm successful snapshots.

Final thought

RDB is not a replacement for application-level backups. Use it as part of a broader recovery plan.

screens.title: How AOF works
screens.narratorSegment: The Append-Only File records every write operation Redis executes. Instead of writing the dataset itself, AOF appends the textual commands that modify state. On restart, Redis reads and replays the AOF sequentially to reconstruct the dataset. This approach reduces the data-loss window because you can choose how often Redis calls fsync to flush buffered writes to disk. AOF has three appendfsync modes: no, everysec, and always. No leaves fsync to the OS, which is fastest but riskiest. Everysec calls fsync once per second, which balances performance and durability and is a common production choice. Always calls fsync on every write, giving the strongest durability but at a performance cost. AOF files grow over time because they contain the full history of writes; BGREWRITEAOF compacts the file by writing the minimal command set needed to rebuild the current dataset. A misconception is that AOF always gives zero data loss — the appendfsync setting determines the actual risk. Understanding how commands are logged and replayed is essential to choosing the right policy. How AOF works means aof appends write commands to a log and replays them on restart; appendfsync controls durability vs performance and bgrewriteaof compacts the file.. In practical terms, logging every write and replaying on startup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Core Concept › How AOF works

Command logging and replay

AOF stores the write commands so a restart can replay them to reconstruct state. This yields finer-grained durability than snapshots.

appendfsync options
  • no: OS controls fsync (fastest, risky)
  • everysec: fsync every second (balanced)
  • always: fsync on every write (durable but slow)
BGREWRITEAOF
Compacts the AOF by writing a minimal set of commands that reconstruct the current dataset, similar to creating a new snapshot for the command log.
Concrete example

Enable appendonly yes and appendfsync everysec. Write commands and examine appendonly.aof to see human-readable commands being appended.

Misconception check

AOF can approach zero data loss, but only with appendfsync always; that setting has a performance cost.

Operational note

Monitor AOF growth and plan rewrites; large AOFs slow recovery because Redis must replay more commands.

screens.title: Configuring AOF and appendfsync

When enabling AOF, also configure appendfilename and ensure the directory has enough space and reliable input and output. After enabling AOF, monitor appendonly. aof growth and plan BGREWRITEAOF to compact it. Testing your configuration is essential: enable AOF, perform writes, check file updates, and simulate a crash to observe recovery behavior. Always match appendfsync to your durability needs and hardware capabilities rather than defaulting without analysis. Process › Configuring AOF

Key config entries

# Example AOF configuration in redis.conf
appendonly yes
appendfilename "appendonly.aof"
appendfsync everysec # Or 'always' or 'no'
  • appendonly yes turns on AOF logging.
  • appendfilename sets the file name on disk.
  • appendfsync controls fsync frequency and durability.
Concrete example

For many systems, appendfsync everysec is a balanced starting point: you get near-real durability with reasonable performance.

Operational warning

Ensure disk space and throughput are sufficient; a full or slow disk will impair Redis performance and risk corruption if uncontrolled.

Monitoring

Track appendonly.aof size and fsync latency. Schedule BGREWRITEAOF when growth exceeds desired multiples of original size.

screens.title: AOF rewrite (BGREWRITEAOF)
screens.narratorSegment: Over time the AOF accumulates a long history of write commands, many of which are redundant. For example, a key that is set multiple times produces multiple entries; compaction removes older redundant commands that are no longer needed to reconstruct the current state. BGREWRITEAOF triggers a rewrite: Redis forks a child process that reads the current in-memory dataset and writes a new minimal AOF containing only the commands necessary to recreate the dataset. When the rewrite finishes, Redis swaps the old AOF with the new compacted file. This reduces disk usage and speeds recovery because there are fewer commands to replay. You can trigger a rewrite manually with BGREWRITEAOF or allow Redis to run it automatically based on file-size growth thresholds. A key operational point is that the rewrite is done by a child process, so it is input and output-heavy but non-blocking for the parent. However, frequent rewrites add C P U and input and output overhead, so tune triggers appropriately. Monitoring AOF size and rewrite frequency helps maintain acceptable recovery times. AOF rewrite (BGREWRITEAOF) means bgrewriteaof forks a child, writes a compact aof representing the current dataset, and replaces the old file to reduce growth and speed recovery.. content.html:
Process Flow › AOF rewrite

Why rewrite matters

Rewriting compacts the AOF to the minimal set of commands needed to recreate the current dataset, reducing disk growth and improving recovery time.

  1. Trigger BGREWRITEAOF manually or via configured thresholds.
  2. Redis forks a child process to read memory and write a new AOF.
  3. When complete, Redis replaces the old AOF with the rewritten one.
Concrete example

Run BGREWRITEAOF after a period of many updates to shrink appendonly.aof and speed future restarts.

Pro tip

Schedule rewrites when the server is quiet to limit resource contention and avoid too-frequent forks.

Monitoring

Watch AOF size and rewrite durations. Very long rewrites indicate you should adjust thresholds or hardware I/O capacity.

screens.title: RDB vs AOF — trade-offs and scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between RDB and AOF depends on how much data loss you can tolerate and how much disk and C P U overhead you accept. RDB is compact and fast to load, making it ideal for periodic backups, fast migrations, and scenarios where small windows of data loss are acceptable — like caching or non-critical session stores. AOF offers finer durability because it logs every write. With appendfsync always you can nearly eliminate data loss, but this slows write performance. appendfsync everysec is a common middle ground. A common production pattern is to enable both: use RDB for reliable, compact backups and AOF to minimize the amount of lost data. Redis prefers AOF during recovery when both files are present because it contains the most recent operations. Misconfiguring appendfsync or forgetting to plan rewrites are frequent operational mistakes. Consider hardware: if disk input and output is limited, AOF always may be unrealistic. The right choice matches application SLAs and the environment's capacity. content.html:
Comparison › RDB vs AOF
When to choose RDB

Backups, fast restarts, and scenarios where occasional data loss is acceptable.

When to choose AOF

Workloads requiring minimal data loss or strict durability guarantees.

Combined approach

Enable both RDB and AOF to get compact backups and low data-loss recovery. Redis will prefer AOF on restart if both exist.

Scenario

A streaming metrics pipeline may accept RDB. Transaction logs for billing should use AOF with a strict fsync policy.

Misconfiguration to avoid

Do not set appendfsync to no for critical data, and do not rely solely on frequent RDB snapshots when minimal loss is required.

screens.title: Using both RDB and AOF together
screens.narratorSegment: Many production deployments enable both RDB and AOF to combine their strengths. RDB provides compact, fast-to-load backups suitable for disaster recovery and point-in-time snapshots. AOF provides a finer-grained command log that reduces the data-loss window. When both are present, Redis chooses the AOF during restart because it contains the most recent operations. The architecture is straightforward: RDB runs on a schedule or on demand, creating dump. rdb snapshots; AOF appends commands continuously to appendonly. aof. In practice, you might schedule snapshots for long-term backups and rely on AOF for incident recovery of recent changes. Be aware of operational coordination: maintain disk space for both files, monitor input and output, and plan BGREWRITEAOF so that AOF growth does not slow recovery. Also test restoring from either file to ensure your recovery plan works. Combining both provides redundancy: if AOF is corrupted but dump. rdb is intact, you still have a recovery option, and vice versa. Using both RDB and AOF together means enable both to get compact backups from rdb and minimal data loss from aof; redis will prefer aof when both files exist during recovery.. In practical terms, combining snapshot backups with write-ahead logging. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Architecture › RDB + AOF together

Redundancy and recovery

Run periodic RDB snapshots for compact backups and enable AOF for continuous logging. Redis loads AOF if available for the most up-to-date state.

Operational checklist
  • Ensure sufficient disk space for both dump.rdb and appendonly.aof.
  • Monitor I/O and schedule BGREWRITEAOF to limit AOF growth.
  • Test restore procedures for both files regularly.
Concrete example

Enable appendonly yes with everysec and also configure save rules for nightly snapshots to retain compact backups while protecting recent changes.

Recovery priority

If both files exist, Redis prefers AOF because it is the most up-to-date representation of operations.

Final tip

Use both for resilience but plan disk, I/O, and rewrite timing so persistence doesn't become a bottleneck.

First, persistence itself means writing volatile in-memory state to disk so it survives crashes and restarts. fullNarratorScript:
In-memory databases deliver speed by keeping data in R A M, but memory is volatile. In this lesson you'll learn the two primary persistence mechanisms Redis provides — RDB snapshots and the Append-Only File — why each exists, and how they trade durability against performance. We'll explore how RDB creates compact, point-in-time binary snapshots using a forked child process, and how AOF logs every write operation so you can replay commands on startup. You will see configuration examples, common mistakes, and a practical hands-on scenario for testing both methods. Knowing these mechanisms helps you design a recovery strategy that meets your application's tolerance for data loss, backup cadence, and performance needs. By the end, you'll be able to choose when to use RDB, when AOF is essential, and why many production deployments enable both. Consider a web session store versus financial events: the right persistence config differs, and we'll make that choice concrete.

In this chapter you will learn to explain why persistence matters for Redis and to configure both RDB snapshots and AOF logging. You will be able to describe how RDB snapshots are created using a forked child process and why that makes snapshots compact and fast to restore. You will also learn how AOF records every write command, how the appendfsync options affect durability and performance, and how AOF rewrite reduces file growth. Practically, you will set up a test redis. conf, enable both persistence modes, write data, simulate a crash, and verify how Redis recovers. Along the way we will discuss common mistakes, like leaving persistence disabled or choosing inappropriate fsync settings, and you will practice interpreting dump. rdb and appendonly. aof. Finally, you will compare scenarios and select a persistence strategy that matches an application's durability and performance needs. Each objective links a concrete skill to why it matters in production.

This second objectives screen emphasizes practice steps and assessment criteria. You will edit redis. conf to add save directives for quick testing, enable appendonly with an appropriate fsync policy, and set file paths so you can find dump. rdb and appendonly. aof. In the lab, you will write sample keys, run BGSAVE and BGREWRITEAOF, and perform a forced crash to verify recovery. For assessment, you should be able to justify a persistence recommendation for a critical workload and explain the AOF rewrite process step-by-step. We will also practice identifying common misconfigurations such as relying on the OS for fsync without understanding the data-loss implications. This focus on concrete hands-on tasks ensures you can reproduce the chapter outcomes in a real environment and reason about trade-offs under real operational constraints. Learning Objectives — Practice & Assessment means hands-on steps and assessment map to configuration, snapshot/rewrite commands, crash simulation, and recovery verification.. In practical terms, lab tasks and assessment alignment. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Redis stores data in memory for speed, but R A M is volatile. If the server crashes or is shut down improperly, data in memory will be lost unless Redis writes state to non-volatile storage. Persistence bridges this gap by ensuring written state survives process restarts and machine failures. There are two primary mechanisms in Redis: RDB snapshots and the Append-Only File. Each takes a different approach. RDB captures a compact point-in-time image of the entire dataset. The result is a single binary snapshot that is fast to load and efficient for backups. AOF, by contrast, records every write command received by the server and replays those commands on restart so the dataset is reconstructed exactly as operations were applied. A common misconception is that enabling any persistence removes all recovery risk; in reality each method offers different guarantees and costs. For example, RDB can lose changes made after the last snapshot, while AOF can be tuned to reduce that window down to zero with higher input and output cost. Understanding this trade-off is the first practical step toward selecting the right configuration for your application.

RDB persists data by creating point-in-time snapshots using a forked child process. When a snapshot is triggered — by a save directive or BGSAVE — the main Redis process forks. The child process serializes the in-memory dataset and writes it to a temporary RDB file on disk. Because of copy-on-write semantics, the parent can continue serving requests while the child performs disk input and output. After the child finishes writing, Redis atomically replaces the old RDB file with the new one. This makes RDB snapshots C P U- and IO-efficient for periodic backups and fast restarts. A key advantage is that the resulting file is compact and quick to load at startup. A key limitation is the data-loss window: any writes after the last snapshot and before a crash are not persisted. Also, frequent snapshots increase disk input and output and the number of forks, which increases C P U usage. For testing you can use save directives like save 900 1 and run BGSAVE manually. Remember a blocking SAVE call will stop the server, so BGSAVE is preferred in production. This explanation clarifies why RDB is ideal for periodic backups, not continuous durability.

RDB is configured with save directives inside redis. conf. Each directive expresses a rule: save. For example, save 900 1 means if at least one key changed within 900 seconds, take a snapshot. You can include multiple save lines to cover different workloads, for instance save 300 10 to capture more frequent changes when many keys update. When designing save rules, balance frequency and overhead: more frequent snapshots reduce your data-loss window but increase disk input and output and C P U work from forking. For testing, set very short rules such as save 5 1 so snapshots occur quickly. Never use the SAVE command in production, because it blocks the server; use BGSAVE instead. Redis supports two snapshot commands with very different operational effects. SAVE writes a snapshot synchronously: the server stops serving clients while it writes dump. rdb. Because of that blocking behavior, SAVE is not recommended in production unless you can tolerate pauses. BGSAVE forks a child process and saves the snapshot in the background, allowing the parent to continue handling requests. The child performs the heavy disk input and output while copy-on-write preserves consistency. A misconception is that both are equivalent except for speed; in reality SAVE can disrupt latency-sensitive services and should be reserved for controlled maintenance windows. BGSAVE has its own costs: each fork increases memory pressure because of copy-on-write, and if the server is already near memory limits, a fork can fail. Use BGSAVE for routine snapshots and plan snapshot frequency to avoid overloading the system. When you need an immediate snapshot for debugging, ensure you understand the production impact before using SAVE. RDB snapshots are compact, fast to load, and excellent for backups and disaster recovery. Because they store a binary representation of the whole dataset, loading dump. rdb at startup reconstructs data quickly from a single file. This makes RDB a great choice when you need periodic backups, want a compact file to transfer between systems, or need fast restart times. The main disadvantage is durability: any writes made after the last snapshot and before a crash will be lost. You can reduce that window by taking snapshots more often, but that increases C P U and disk activity. Another risk is that frequent forks increase memory pressure due to copy-on-write and can create performance spikes. Common use cases for RDB include scheduled backups, exporting datasets, and environments where occasional small data loss is acceptable, such as caches or analytics that can be recomputed. A misconception is treating RDB as sufficient for all production durability needs — for strong durability guarantees, combine RDB with AOF or tune AOF for your workload. The Append-Only File records every write operation Redis executes. Instead of writing the dataset itself, AOF appends the textual commands that modify state. On restart, Redis reads and replays the AOF sequentially to reconstruct the dataset. This approach reduces the data-loss window because you can choose how often Redis calls fsync to flush buffered writes to disk. AOF has three appendfsync modes: no, everysec, and always. No leaves fsync to the OS, which is fastest but riskiest. Everysec calls fsync once per second, which balances performance and durability and is a common production choice. Always calls fsync on every write, giving the strongest durability but at a performance cost. AOF files grow over time because they contain the full history of writes; BGREWRITEAOF compacts the file by writing the minimal command set needed to rebuild the current dataset. A misconception is that AOF always gives zero data loss — the appendfsync setting determines the actual risk. Over time the AOF accumulates a long history of write commands, many of which are redundant. For example, a key that is set multiple times produces multiple entries; compaction removes older redundant commands that are no longer needed to reconstruct the current state. BGREWRITEAOF triggers a rewrite: Redis forks a child process that reads the current in-memory dataset and writes a new minimal AOF containing only the commands necessary to recreate the dataset. When the rewrite finishes, Redis swaps the old AOF with the new compacted file. This reduces disk usage and speeds recovery because there are fewer commands to replay. You can trigger a rewrite manually with BGREWRITEAOF or allow Redis to run it automatically based on file-size growth thresholds. A key operational point is that the rewrite is done by a child process, so it is input and output-heavy but non-blocking for the parent. However, frequent rewrites add C P U and input and output overhead, so tune triggers appropriately. Monitoring AOF size and rewrite frequency helps maintain acceptable recovery times. Choosing between RDB and AOF depends on how much data loss you can tolerate and how much disk and C P U overhead you accept. RDB is compact and fast to load, making it ideal for periodic backups, fast migrations, and scenarios where small windows of data loss are acceptable — like caching or non-critical session stores. AOF offers finer durability because it logs every write. With appendfsync always you can nearly eliminate data loss, but this slows write performance. appendfsync everysec is a common middle ground. A common production pattern is to enable both: use RDB for reliable, compact backups and AOF to minimize the amount of lost data. Redis prefers AOF during recovery when both files are present because it contains the most recent operations. Misconfiguring appendfsync or forgetting to plan rewrites are frequent operational mistakes. Consider hardware: if disk input and output is limited, AOF always may be unrealistic. The right choice matches application SLAs and the environment's capacity.
